summary: A lamb leg mini roast — the small boneless piece of leg Australian supermarkets sell for two — rubbed with rosemary, garlic, honey and dijon mustard, roasted on a rack over its own vegetables, then sliced. A carved roast for a weeknight, in under an hour: smaller than a whole leg, and roasted hot rather than slowly.

ingredients.note: The source gives no weight. Read it off the label; the timing in the yield note goes by weight. Check whether it is tied or netted — see the safety notes.

ingredients.quantity: To serve; optional in the source.

method.instruction: Set a rack in a baking dish and put the lamb on it. The source gives no dish size; one that holds the rack with room for the vegetables underneath and around it will do.
Mix the rosemary, oil, honey, mustard and garlic and rub it all over the lamb. The source makes a 20-minute rest in the fridge to marinate optional.

Heat the oven to 200°C. The source calls this a hot oven and gives no fan or conventional label, and no second figure is invented here. The source names no shelf; a middle shelf is this project's ordinary default, not a source instruction.
Roast the lamb for 10 minutes. Then put the potatoes, pumpkin and onion into the same dish and roast for 20 minutes more.
Add the zucchini and tomatoes and roast for a further 10 to 15 minutes, until the lamb is done the way you like it. A heavier roast will need longer; see the yield note.

Measure in the thickest part of the roast, through to the middle. If the roast is an untied, unrolled piece of leg, Health Canada's lowest figure for a whole lamb cut is 63°C internal (medium-rare), and Australian Lamb's doneness guide — about eating quality, not safety — gives 65 to 70°C for medium, pink throughout. If it has been rolled and tied or netted, FSANZ recommends at least 75°C in the centre for rolled roasts. Australian Lamb suggests taking lamb out about 3 to 6°C before your goal, as it keeps cooking while it rests.
Cover the lamb with foil and rest it for 5 minutes, then slice it across the grain and serve with the vegetables, and mint sauce if you like.

yield_note: Serves 2, as stated by the source. Source times: 10 minutes preparation and 45 minutes cooking; the steps add up to 40 to 45 minutes in the oven and 5 minutes' rest. The source also gives a rule of 50 to 60 minutes per kg for the lamb. By this project's arithmetic from that rule, not by a source statement, that is about 40 to 48 minutes for an 800 g roast and 50 to 60 minutes for a 1 kg roast; the vegetables can go in at the same points, counted back from the end. A larger roast is one way to have cold lamb left for the next day. Times are a guide only: the thermometer decides.

provenance_note: Recipe facts paraphrased from the Women's Weekly Food page, accessed 2026-10-06. The source's doneness cue is 'cooked to taste'; the temperatures in this record are not the source's, and each is credited to the guide it comes from. The source does not say whether its mini roast is tied or netted. Because FSANZ treats rolled roasts like mince and gives them a higher figure, the record states both cases rather than guessing which one the reader has bought. The source gives no roast weight and no fan figure; the per-weight times in the yield note are this project's arithmetic from the source's own per-kg rule.

caveats: Shopping names: a lamb leg mini roast (迷你羊腿烤肉) is a small boneless piece of leg; it may also be labelled a boneless leg portion. A half leg roast (半只羊腿) is bigger and often bone-in; it is not what this source was written for. The source's per-kg rule is the only timing it gives, and the thermometer decides.

Rolled or not decides the figure. FSANZ recommends at least 75°C in the centre for rolled roasts, along with mince and sausages. This project's reading of why: rolling folds the outside of the meat into the middle. A single unrolled piece is a whole cut: Health Canada's lowest figure for that is 63°C internal (medium-rare), and FSANZ gives 70°C in the centre as a general figure that will help ensure food is safe.
Australian Lamb's doneness temperatures describe eating quality. Its rare figure, 60°C, is below both safety figures above.

Leftovers: slice cold lamb off the roast, get it into the fridge within 2 hours — FSANZ says cooked food out for less than 2 hours can go back in the fridge — keep it at 5°C or colder and use it within a few days. Eat it cold, or reheat it until the centre reaches 74°C (Health Canada's figure for leftovers).
This record has had no professional food-safety review and has not been kitchen-tested by this project.
